questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Executive pressure on a constitutional court
questions.learningObjective: Identify the mechanism by which an executive can pressure a constitutional court.
questions.stem: In my observing log, the Meridian Astronomical Society's arbitration panel refused to certify the committee's allocation of telescope time, and the committee then quietly reopened the appointments list.

options.text: Control over appointments lets the committee steer the panel without issuing any order
The panel exceeded its remit, since observing time is a matter for the committee
options.misconception: treats a tribunal's ruling as an absence of jurisdiction

options.text: Any member may reopen the appointments list, so no pressure has been applied
options.misconception: confuses a general membership power with executive pressure

options.text: The dispute concerns the committee's competence, not the panel's independence
options.misconception: reframes the independence question as a competence question

questions.explanation: Executive pressure on a court works through appointment, funding and reputation rather than orders. Here the committee can name the panel, so it can shape the panel's future without telling any member how to rule.
questions.hint: Ask which lever the committee actually controls.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Entrenchment as protection against the founders
questions.learningObjective: Explain how entrenched amendment rules protect a constitution from its own founders.
questions.stem: My log for the Ridgecrest Observatory Club notes that the founders' charter cannot be altered by a simple majority of the present membership.

options.text: The charter requires unanimity, so no amendment could ever be carried
options.misconception: confuses entrenchment with a veto no coalition can pass

options.text: The charter needs a supermajority, which shields the settlement from a temporary majority
The charter is defended by a court that strikes down any amendment attempt
options.misconception: credits judicial review instead of amendment procedure

options.text: The charter survives because the founders may veto any later change themselves
options.misconception: assumes the original drafters keep a standing veto

questions.explanation: Entrenchment raises the cost of amendment so that a fleeting majority of the founders' own generation cannot rewrite the settlement. It is a procedural shield, not a veto held by particular people.
questions.hint: Focus on how hard amendment is, not on who votes.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Two-thirds arithmetic in a chamber
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the two-thirds threshold in a chamber and the votes it leaves.
questions.stem: The Halcyon Chamber's division list shows sixty-one members voting on the water charter: forty-one for, twenty against, with no abstentions, and the rule requires two-thirds of those voting.

options.text: The charter passed, because forty-one meets the two-thirds threshold of forty-one votes
The charter failed, because two-thirds of the full membership would be eighty votes
options.misconception: applies the threshold to membership rather than to voters

options.text: The charter passed, because a bare majority of the sixty-one voting carries it
options.misconception: applies a bare majority rule to a supermajority question

options.text: The charter failed, because the twenty opposed votes exceeded the allowed margin of ten
options.misconception: invents a margin limit the rule does not contain

questions.explanation: Two-thirds of sixty-one is 40.67, so forty-one votes satisfy the rule without any fraction left over. The threshold applies to those who voted, so the full membership does not enter the calculation.
questions.hint: Multiply two-thirds by the number who voted.

questions.topic: Tracing a decision through weakened checks
questions.learningObjective: Trace how a policy reaches enactment when intermediate checks are removed.
questions.stem: Tracing the Atlas Observatory's flow chart: the executive board drafts policy, sends it to the assembly, the assembly votes once, and the board's nominees confirm it. Where did the check fail?

options.text: The executive board can now write the rules itself, since the assembly rubber-stamps them
options.misconception: stops at the first step and ignores the confirming stage

options.text: The assembly's vote is the weak link, since one chamber cannot check a single board
options.misconception: blames voting procedure rather than the missing stage

options.text: The nominees' confirmation is too slow, so decisions arrive after the scrutiny
options.misconception: mistakes delay in confirmation for absence of scrutiny

options.text: The missing second reading breaks the return path, so nothing can send the policy back

questions.explanation: With only one reading and no review stage, a flawed policy travels straight from board to enactment. Removing the return path between the two institutions is what severs the check.
questions.hint: Ask what stage could have sent the policy back.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The credible alternative as a check
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a check operates only where the alternative is credible.
questions.stem: When the Greyhollow Society's president had no alternative to the assembly's budget bill, she signed it within the hour. Explain what that shows about the strength of her check.

answer.exemplar: A veto or a suspensive vote bites only when the executive has a course that is worse than compliance. Here refusing meant the society would have had no money at all, an outcome both sides wanted to avoid, so the bill was not chosen because the assembly's reasoning persuaded the president but because refusal was the costlier path. The president therefore had no leverage and the signature registered assent rather than agreement. The general lesson is that formal powers are cheap to grant and expensive to use, and their value is determined by the alternatives they open up.

questions.explanation: A check operates only when refusal carries consequences the executive would rather avoid. Here refusal produced the outcome the president wanted least, so the signature recorded assent rather than agreement.
questions.hint: Ask what refusing would have cost the president.

options.misconception: reads a coercive presence as routine protection

options.text: The deployment shows the count was inconclusive, so troops stepped in to break it
options.misconception: invents a disputed count the source never mentions

questions.stem: Given the passage from my night notes, which criticism of the Silver Ridge settlement does the passage itself raise?

options.misconception: reverses the direction of the imbalance described

options.misconception: invents a claim about symmetry the passage rejects

options.text: The settlement weakened the older families, because landholding rules were set nationally
options.misconception: inverts the passage's account of who benefited

questions.explanation: The passage says the bargain kept old regional landholding law and limited the centre, which critics read as preserving older families' advantage. The criticism concerns who the settlement favoured.

options.misconception: treats a supermajority as a minority veto power

options.text: The two-thirds rule raises the votes needed without changing who can win
options.misconception: ignores the way a threshold reshapes coalitions

The two-thirds rule makes ordinary majority voting impossible for all business

options.misconception: treats speed as the only measure of institutional health

options.misconception: infers the strength of a threat from the target's resolve

The printing of the first ballot papers, since it commits the guild to the original date

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Military deployment at the polls
questions.learningObjective: Explain how troop deployment at polling stations undermines electoral freedom.
questions.stem: At the Beacon Hill Institute's election, soldiers stood within sight of the ballot tables for three hours. Explain what this does to the freedom of the vote.

answer.exemplar: Freedom of the vote is a condition about how choices are made, not merely about whether ballots are eventually counted. Soldiers stationed near the tables change how voters behave even when no order is given: a voter who sees force may conceal a genuine preference, abandon the queue, or settle for the candidate they judge safest. Each of those is a way in which the result reflects the presence of troops rather than the programmes on offer, so the deployment is capable of shaping the outcome without falsifying a single ballot. This is why the presence of armed personnel at a polling place is treated as a substantive threat to the vote rather than as neutral assistance with the administration.

questions.explanation: Freedom of the vote concerns how choices are made, not merely whether ballots are counted. Visible force near the tables coerces some voters and so undermines the free character of the election.
questions.hint: Consider what a voter feels when soldiers stand nearby.

questions.stem: Given the passage from the Larkspur charter, what is the effect of the rule described for Article 9?

options.text: It gives the three branches a permanent veto, since each can refuse its assent forever
options.misconception: converts a numerical threshold into a standing veto

options.text: It protects the original settlement by making amendment much harder than ordinary change
It lets a simple majority amend Article 9 after three branches have been consulted
options.misconception: invents consultation in place of the required assent

options.text: It expires automatically once the branches grow beyond their original size
options.misconception: invents an automatic expiry the charter does not contain

questions.explanation: Requiring a supermajority plus the assent of every branch makes Article 9 far harder to change than ordinary charter provisions. This is the classic pattern of entrenchment protecting a founders' settlement.

options.misconception: computes two-thirds of those present rather than all members

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Executive pressure on a constitutional court
questions.learningObjective: Explain how appointments and funding together shape a court's independence.
questions.stem: At Meridian, the arbitration panel has three of its nine seats filled by the committee, and the committee also pays the panel's expenses. Explain what this arrangement does to the panel's independence.

answer.exemplar: Independence here is a matter of how the panel would reason if a ruling went against the committee, and this arrangement puts pressure on that reasoning without ever threatening it. The committee appoints a third of the panel and pays its costs, so a ruling favourable to the committee would please both the people who name its members and the people who fund it. Nothing requires the committee to interfere, and no interference would be needed for the structure to shape decisions: the panel would learn to discount the risk of disagreement rather than have that risk imposed on it. A panel is independent when the cost of deciding against the powerful is borne by the panel and not by it.

questions.explanation: Control over appointments and funding shapes the risk a panel faces even if no one intervenes. Independence turns on who bears the cost of an unfavourable ruling, not on whether pressure was applied.
questions.hint: Ask who bears the cost of an unfavourable ruling.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Two-thirds arithmetic in a chamber
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a supermajority rule broadens the coalition needed to govern.
questions.stem: The Aster Valley Council must now pass every budget by a three-fifths majority instead of a simple majority. Explain what this does to the kind of coalition that can govern.

answer.exemplar: A three-fifths threshold cannot be cleared by a bare majority, so no party holding a small majority can govern on its own. The largest bloc must now attract support from outside its own ranks, either by reaching an agreement with a smaller party or by persuading members to cross the floor. The rule therefore changes the incentives of negotiation: every governing coalition must be broader and more durable than the one a simple majority would allow, and a government that loses that support faces defeat sooner than before. Critics also note the trade-off, since the same requirement makes it harder to remove a government that has lost its mandate, but the dominant effect is on the breadth of coalition required.

questions.explanation: Raising the threshold means a governing coalition must include voters beyond its own majority. It rewards negotiation and broadens the coalition that must be assembled for any budget to pass.
questions.hint: Ask who can now be left out of a working majority.

questions.topic: The credible alternative as a check

questions.stem: In my log, the Greyhollow Society's president vetoed the assembly's harbour levy and announced she would hold a referendum on the levy itself. Explain what determined whether that veto could work.

answer.exemplar: Whether a veto can work depends on what follows for the other side if it is used, and here the president has offered the assembly an alternative rather than a threat: a referendum, which the members may prefer to the levy. If the assembly believes the referendum would produce a worse settlement, the veto has force, because accepting the levy becomes the less costly course. If members would welcome the referendum, the veto amounts to a preference with no leverage behind it. The mechanism is the same one that operates where a president threatens to refer a bill to the electorate, and in both cases the president is strong only where the electorate's answer is one the assembly would rather avoid.

questions.explanation: A veto works only where the other side prefers the alternative to compliance. The referendum bites only if the assembly regards it as the outcome it would rather avoid.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Tracing a decision through weakened checks
questions.learningObjective: Identify the effect of merging a review body into the body it reviewed.
questions.stem: The Verity Observatory Society has merged its review committee into the executive board, and board members now review their own spending.

options.text: The merge has weakened the check, since the reviewing body is now chaired by the executive
options.misconception: assumes a chairmanship rule the entry does not state

options.text: The merge has weakened the check, since reviews now happen more frequently each year
options.misconception: invents a change in frequency the entry does not mention

options.text: The merge has strengthened the check, since the board holds full information on every item
options.misconception: treats information held by the body as independent review

options.text: The merge has removed the check, since a body cannot review its own conduct

questions.explanation: A check requires someone outside the body being checked. Placing the review inside the executive board removes the possibility of that review being independent, whatever the board's own diligence.
questions.hint: Ask who is now checking the executive.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: The credible alternative as a check
questions.learningObjective: Compare two assemblies to locate where a veto took effect.
questions.stem: My log compares two Greyhollow assemblies. In the first, the president had no alternative to the assembly's bill and signed it within the hour. In the second, she refused and put the matter to the members, and the assembly then amended its own bill to meet her terms.

options.text: The second assembly was stronger, since it amended a bill rather than being overridden
options.misconception: treats a negotiated amendment as a defeat for the executive

options.text: The president's refusal worked because the assembly had a worse option than compliance
The president's refusal failed, since the assembly still passed a version of its own bill
options.misconception: treats any agreement as a defeat for the veto

options.text: The two assemblies differed only in their size, since membership was the same in both
options.misconception: invents a variable the entry holds constant

questions.explanation: In the first case the president had no alternative and the bill passed unopposed; in the second she had one, and the assembly's willingness to amend shows it preferred that alternative to the original terms.
questions.hint: Ask which side had the worse option in each case.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Postponing a scheduled election
questions.learningObjective: Identify the decision point in a sequence of postponement steps.
questions.stem: My sketch of the Northlight Guild's deferral runs: date announced, ballot papers printed, a committee resolution postpones the poll, new date set sixty days later, ballots reprinted and dispatched.

options.text: The committee resolution is the decision point, since everything before it is preparation
The printing of the first ballot papers is the decision point, since it commits the guild
options.misconception: mistakes routine preparation for the binding decision

options.text: The setting of the new date is the decision point, since that is when the change takes effect
options.misconception: locates the choice in the later scheduling step

options.text: The announcement of the original date is the decision point, since publicity began it
options.misconception: treats an announcement as though it decided the outcome

questions.explanation: Preparatory steps can proceed under any date, so only the resolution that defers the poll is the point of choice. Everything after it, including reprinting and dispatching the ballots, implements a decision already taken.
questions.hint: Ask which step could have been followed by another date.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Military deployment at the polls
questions.learningObjective: Explain how visible force at a poll restricts the freedom of choice.
questions.stem: At the Halcyon Institute's assembly election, soldiers of the county regiment were assigned to guard the ballot tables for the whole day, and the returning officer asked for no explanation. Explain what this does to the freedom of the vote.

answer.exemplar: Freedom of the vote is a condition about how the choice is made, not merely about whether the ballots are eventually counted. Soldiers standing at the tables for the whole of polling day put a visible armed presence between the voter and the act of voting itself. No threat need be made and no ballot need be falsified for that presence to matter: a voter who sees force at the booth may conceal a preference, abandon the queue, or vote for what they think is safe, and each of those is a way of the result being shaped by the deployment rather than by the candidates. The absence of any request for a reason adds to the problem, since it leaves the members unable to judge whether the presence served any legitimate purpose at all.

questions.explanation: Freedom of the vote concerns how choices are made, not merely whether ballots are counted. Visible force at the tables coerces some voters and so undermines the free character of the election.
questions.hint: Consider what a voter feels when soldiers stand nearby.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Criticism of a founding settlement
questions.learningObjective: Count the clauses left open to amendment in an entrenched charter.
questions.stem: In the Silver Ridge Federation's charter, twelve founding clauses are listed and four of them are entrenched, requiring a three-fourths vote to amend. How many clauses may be amended by a simple majority?
questions.explanation: Twelve listed clauses less the four entrenched ones leaves eight open to ordinary amendment. The criticism of such settlements turns on part of the original text being unreachable by a current majority.
questions.hint: Subtract the entrenched clauses from the total.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Executive pressure on a constitutional court
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish informal executive pressure from a formal legal power.

stimulus.body: Extract from the Brackenhill Society's gazette, March: The president has asked the arbitration panel to reconsider its ruling in the matter of the telescope allocation, observing that the panel's decision has cost the society two observatory sites. The gazette records that the president's request has no formal standing in the society's rules.

questions.stem: According to the gazette extract, what does the president's request demonstrate?

options.text: That the president can overturn the panel's ruling whenever the society suffers
options.misconception: assumes a power the extract expressly denies

options.text: That the gazette treats the panel's ruling as a matter for the general membership
options.misconception: infers a referral to members the extract does not mention

options.text: That executive disapproval can reach a court informally, without any legal power
That disputes over telescope allocation are beyond the panel's competence
options.misconception: reads a presidential request as a ruling on jurisdiction

questions.explanation: The gazette states that the request has no formal standing, so the president cannot lawfully direct the panel. Yet the pressure is real, which is exactly how informal executive influence over a court operates.
questions.hint: Note what the gazette says about the request's standing.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Entrenchment as protection against the founders
questions.learningObjective: Recognise an entrenched clause and the protection it gives the settlement.

stimulus.body: From the Larkspur Society's charter: Article 9 may not be repealed, and any attempt to alter it requires the assent of two-thirds of the membership and of the council of each of the three branches. The drafters added this in the first decade, when the society was still small and personal.

questions.stem: On the strength of the Larkspur charter passage, what does the rule laid down for Article 9 actually do?

options.text: It gives the three branches a permanent veto, since each can refuse its assent forever
options.misconception: converts a numerical threshold into a standing veto

options.text: It protects the original settlement by making amendment much harder than ordinary change
It lets a simple majority amend Article 9 after three branches have been consulted
options.misconception: invents consultation in place of the required assent

options.text: It expires automatically once the branches grow beyond their original size
options.misconception: invents an automatic expiry the charter does not contain

questions.explanation: Requiring a supermajority plus the assent of every branch makes Article 9 far harder to change than ordinary charter provisions. This is the classic pattern of entrenchment protecting a founders' settlement.
questions.hint: Compare the rule for Article 9 with ordinary change.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Two-thirds arithmetic in a chamber
questions.learningObjective: Design a voting rule that combines broad agreement with a quorum.
questions.stem: My log asks which arrangement best lets a divided chamber make difficult decisions while keeping broad agreement. Which rule fits?

options.text: A two-thirds majority of members present, with a quorum of half the membership
A simple majority of members present, since a bare majority settles most business
options.misconception: offers a rule that provides no extra agreement

options.text: Unanimity of all members, since only complete agreement removes the risk of error
options.misconception: demands agreement that would make the chamber unusable

options.text: A two-thirds majority of the full membership, regardless of how many attend
options.misconception: ignores the quorum and so blocks decisions by absence

questions.explanation: A two-thirds threshold of those present demands broad agreement without letting a small attendance decide for the chamber, and a quorum of half the membership prevents that abuse. Unanimity makes the chamber unusable.
questions.hint: Ask what stops a handful deciding for the chamber.

questions.subject: COMPARATIVE_GOVERNMENT
questions.topic: Tracing a decision through weakened checks
questions.learningObjective: Identify which check a change of default procedure has hollowed out.
questions.stem: First, in the Oakvale Trust a measure of the executive board needed a second reading by the assembly. Second, the standing orders now provide that a measure takes effect if the assembly does not object within one sitting. Which check has been weakened?

options.text: The assembly's power to call a special sitting, which the new standing orders remove
options.misconception: invents a change the new orders do not make

options.text: The second reading, since a measure now takes effect unless the assembly objects in time
The executive's duty to report, since reporting is no longer required at all
options.misconception: removes a duty the new orders keep

options.text: The assembly's membership, since the new orders cut the number of members
options.misconception: invents a change to membership the orders do not make

questions.explanation: A second reading lets the assembly stop a measure. Replacing it with a rule that a measure takes effect unless objected to in time shifts the burden onto the assembly and removes the veto it held.
questions.hint: Ask what the assembly can no longer do to a measure.
